transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

Uh... just having some trouble, I guess. It's just... I always feel like I got this motor running inside me. All day. 

If I have to sit still—like at church, or out there in the clinic waiting room, or even just at home—I just... I feel trapped. I always gotta get up or do something.
When did you first start noticing this feeling of having a motor running inside you? Was it something you've had since you were a kid, or did it start more recently?

Uh... guess it's been a long time. Since I was a boy. 

Back in school... teachers were always moving my seat around. I just... couldn't stay put. I'd talk out of turn, get in trouble for jumping up before class was even done. So... yeah. Always been like that, I guess.

Besides the restlessness and needing to move around, do you also have trouble focusing or paying attention to things? Like, do you find it hard to concentrate on tasks, or do you get easily distracted?

I guess so. Uh... like when folks are talking... going over ride times, or lists for the pantry. Or church plans. 

I listen good at first, but... I don't know. My mind just slips off. I end up missing pieces I really needed to hear. So... yeah.
Do you find yourself doing things without thinking first? Like, do you act on impulse, interrupt people, or make quick decisions you later regret?

I guess so. Uh... I do jump in a lot. Like... if my cousin's talking. Or the pastor... or the lady down at the pantry. 

I just... I spit out an answer before they're even done talking. Then... well, I realize I said the wrong thing. Or they just get mad at me. So... yeah.
You mentioned this has been going on since you were a boy. Is that restless feeling—that motor running inside you—still just as strong now as it was back then, or has it gotten better over the years?

Uh... I don't really know. Ain't much for comparing, I guess. 

It's... still there. Still always feel like I gotta be moving or doing something. So... guess it ain't got much better. Just... about the same.
Has this trouble with sitting still, focusing, and jumping in—has it caused you real problems in your life? Like, has it affected your job, relationships, or how you get along with people?

Yeah... I suppose. 

Folks... they don't really trust me with stuff no more. Like at the church, or the pantry... even my family. Just... they won't let me handle the rides, or the supplies. Say I mess up the appointments. 

I try to help out, but... I don't know. I just end up letting everybody down, I guess. So... yeah. It causes problems.
When you think back to school and even now... which was harder for you—sitting still and not moving around, or actually paying attention and keeping your mind on what you were supposed to be doing?

I guess... maybe paying attention is harder. 

Like... when they're talking at the church, or... going over the lists for the pantry. Or the ride times. I try to listen. I do. But... my mind just sort of slips off after a minute. 

I hear the start of it, and then... I just miss the rest. The pieces I was supposed to remember. So... yeah. Probably that.

Right now, today—when you're going about your day—is that restless feeling, that need to be moving and doing something, still as much of a problem for you as the trouble paying attention? Or is it more the attention piece that gets in your way now?

Uh... I guess they're both pretty bad. 

That... that motor feeling... it's just going all day. If I have to sit still anywhere... like at the church, or... waiting out there at the clinic, or even just at the house... I don't know. I just feel trapped. 

I can't stand it. I just have to get up or... do something. So... yeah. It's still a problem.

Back when you were in school, was that restless feeling—needing to move around and not being able to sit still—pretty much the same as it is now? Or has that part gotten noticeably better as you've gotten older?

I guess... it's about the same. 

Back then... teachers were always moving my desk around. I couldn't just sit there. I'd talk when I wasn't supposed to, or... I'd just get up before it was time to go. Got in trouble a lot for it. 

So... I don't know that it's any better now. Just... different places I have to sit.

When you think about the problems you're having now at church, the pantry, and with your family—is it more the restless feeling and needing to move around that's causing the mess-ups, or is it more the trouble paying attention and forgetting what you're supposed to do?

I guess... it's kind of both. 

They... they don't really trust me with things anymore. The people at church, or... the pantry. My family, too. I mess up the rides, or I forget the appointments. I lose track of the supplies. 

I don't mean to. I want to help them. But... I just keep letting everybody down. So... yeah. It's all of it.

When you think back to your school days and even now... if you could somehow fix just the restless feeling—that motor inside you—but still had trouble paying attention... do you think that would solve most of your problems? Or would you still be running into the same kinds of trouble?

I don't... I really don't know. I never thought about it like that. 

I guess... I'd probably still mess things up if I couldn't pay attention. But... I'm not sure. It's hard to say.

Back when you were in school—when the teachers kept moving your desk around and you were getting in trouble—what was the main reason they were frustrated with you? Was it mainly because you couldn't sit still and kept moving around, or was it more because you weren't paying attention in class?

I mean... like I said a minute ago. It was mostly the moving around. 

I just couldn't stay put. That's why they were always moving my seat... because I'd talk out of turn, or just jump up before class was even done. That was the main thing they got mad at.

When you were in school and the teachers were moving your seat around—was the main problem that you couldn't sit still and had to move around, or was it also that you were having trouble paying attention to what they were teaching?

I... I just said that. It was the moving around. 

I couldn't stay put. They moved my seat because I wouldn't stay in it. I'd talk when I wasn't supposed to, or... just get up and leave before we were even done. That's what I got in trouble for.

Back in school, when you couldn't sit still and were talking out of turn—were you also having trouble actually paying attention to what the teacher was teaching? Or was it mainly just the sitting still part that was the problem?

Look... I just answered this. It was the sitting still. 

I don't really know if I was paying attention or not. I just remember I couldn't stay in the chair. That's all I remember.

When you were in school and having all those troubles—do you remember if you had a hard time keeping your mind on schoolwork and assignments, or was it really just about not being able to sit still in your seat?
I... I don't know. Like I said, I just remember the chair thing. I don't really remember the rest of it.

Right now, in your daily life—when you're at church, the pantry, or helping your family—which one causes you more trouble: that restless motor feeling where you can't sit still, or the trouble keeping your mind on what you're supposed to be doing?

I don't know... it's just... it's both, I guess, but it messes everything up. 

People at the church... they don't ask me to drive anymore. The pantry, too. They stopped trusting me with the supplies and... keeping track of appointments and stuff. My family... it's the same. I just... I keep letting everybody down. I mean to help, I really do, but... it just doesn't work out.

When you were in school and couldn't sit still in your seat—do you also remember having trouble keeping your mind on the schoolwork itself? Like, when you were supposed to be doing assignments or reading, could you focus on that, or did your mind wander a lot back then too?

I don't know why you keep asking me the same thing. I told you... I don't remember the schoolwork part. 

It was a long time ago and I didn't even stay in school that long anyway. I just remember I couldn't stay in the chair. I don't know where my mind was. That's it.
Right now, today—which one gets you in more trouble: jumping in and talking before people finish, or forgetting things and losing track of what you're supposed to be doing?

I guess... the talking part. 

I just... I jump in before people are done. Like with the pastor, or my cousin... or the lady at the pantry. I just say the answer before they finish asking. And then... I realize I said the wrong thing, or I just made them mad. It just comes out.

Right now, in your daily life—is that restless feeling, that motor running inside you, still causing you as much trouble as it did back in school? Or has that part gotten a bit easier to manage as you've gotten older?

I don't know about easier... it's still there. That's why I'm here, I guess. 

It's just... like a motor running inside me all day. If I have to sit still... like at church, or waiting out there in the clinic, or even just at home... I can't. I just feel trapped. I have to get up and do something. It doesn't stop.

In the last few years—say, the last couple of years—when you're at church, the pantry, or helping your family... is that restless feeling and needing to move around still just as strong as it was back when you were in school? Or has that part calmed down some, even though you're still having other troubles?

I don't think it's calmed down. It's... it's been real hard to handle lately. For about two years now. Maybe two years and a couple months. 

Ever since... well, an older relative of mine, their health changed. I had to start doing more... taking on more stuff for them. So... yeah. It's still just as bad.

target_item.reason: The doctor's question asks to compare two current symptoms: 'jumping in and talking before people finish' (S016: Blurting_Answers) or 'forgetting things and losing track of what you're supposed to be doing' (S002/S004/S005). I will select S016 to address the 'jumping in and talking' aspect.

patient.answer:
I guess... the talking part. 

I just... I jump in before people are done. Like with the pastor, or my cousin... or the lady at the pantry. I just say the answer before they finish asking. And then... I realize I said the wrong thing, or I just made them mad. It just comes out.

doctor.intent: Determine whether hyperactivity/restlessness is currently the predominant symptom (F90.1 - predominantly hyperactive-impulsive type) or whether inattention is equally or more prominent (F90.9 - unspecified type), by asking about the relative severity of hyperactivity symptoms in the present day.
doctor.question: Right now, in your daily life—is that restless feeling, that motor running inside you, still causing you as much trouble as it did back in school? Or has that part gotten a bit easier to manage as you've gotten older?

target_item.name: Feeling_Restless
target_item.manifestation: I came in because I feel like I got a motor running inside me all day, and if I have to sit still at church, at the clinic, or at home, I feel trapped and have to get up or do something.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking specifically about the restless feeling, the 'motor running inside', and whether it is still causing trouble now compared to back in school.

patient.answer:
I don't know about easier... it's still there. That's why I'm here, I guess. 

It's just... like a motor running inside me all day. If I have to sit still... like at church, or waiting out there in the clinic, or even just at home... I can't. I just feel trapped. I have to get up and do something. It doesn't stop.

doctor.intent: Determine whether hyperactivity symptoms have persisted into adulthood at the same level of severity as in childhood, or whether inattention has become the more prominent symptom in recent years—this distinction separates predominantly hyperactive-impulsive type (F90.1) from predominantly inattentive type (F90.9).
doctor.question: In the last few years—say, the last couple of years—when you're at church, the pantry, or helping your family... is that restless feeling and needing to move around still just as strong as it was back when you were in school? Or has that part calmed down some, even though you're still having other troubles?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: It has been this hard to manage for about two years and two months, ever since my older relative’s health changed and I had to take on more responsibilities.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the timeline of the symptoms, specifically referring to the "last few years" or "last couple of years" to understand how long the current level of restlessness has been present.

patient.answer:
I don't think it's calmed down. It's... it's been real hard to handle lately. For about two years now. Maybe two years and a couple months. 

Ever since... well, an older relative of mine, their health changed. I had to start doing more... taking on more stuff for them. So... yeah. It's still just as bad.

opening_question.intent: Establish rapport and identify the chief complaint that brings the patient to the psychiatric clinic today
opening_question.question: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient presents with lifelong history of hyperactivity-impulsivity symptoms (motor restlessness, inability to sit still, talking out of turn, interrupting) since childhood, with prominent inattention symptoms currently (difficulty maintaining focus during conversations, forgetting appointments and details). The clinical presentation is predominantly characterized by hyperactivity-impulsivity in childhood school records (teachers moving seat, talking out of turn, jumping up) with inattention becoming more salient in current functioning. Significant functional impairment documented across multiple domains (church roles, pantry work, family relationships, loss of trust). Duration exceeds 20+ years with persistent symptoms into adulthood. Meets criteria for ADHD, Combined Presentation with hyperactivity-impulsivity as the primary historical feature, now manifesting as F90.1 (ADHD predominantly hyperactive-impulsive type).
